mcqs.question: Before OAuth, a third-party app would ask users for their actual username and password on another service to access their data. What is the core problem with this approach?
options: It's slower than modern token-based approaches
It requires the third-party app to store data in an unencrypted format
It doesn't work for mobile applications at all
The third-party app gains a credential that can do everything the account can do, and can't be selectively revoked without changing the password everywhere
mcqs.explanation: Handing over the actual password gives the third-party app unlimited, unscoped access indistinguishable from the real user's own login, and the only way to cut off that access is changing the password everywhere it's used. Speed isn't the core issue, this anti-pattern was actually common in mobile apps too, and it says nothing about how data is stored afterward.

mcqs.question: In OAuth terminology, which role is the third-party application requesting access to a user's data?
options: The Resource Owner
The Authorization Server
The Client
The Resource Server
mcqs.explanation: The 'Client' in OAuth specifically means the requesting application — not a client in the general client-server sense — which is a common source of confusion. The Resource Owner is the user, the Authorization Server authenticates the user and issues tokens, and the Resource Server holds the actual protected data.

mcqs.question: In the Authorization Code grant, why does the Client exchange the authorization code for an access token via a direct server-to-server call, rather than receiving the token through the browser redirect?
options: Server-to-server calls are always faster than browser redirects
Browsers are technically incapable of receiving an access token in a URL
It keeps the access token itself off the browser entirely — only the short-lived, single-use code travels through the redirect, which is safer if exposed
It allows the Authorization Server to skip verifying the user's identity
mcqs.explanation: Routing the actual token exchange server-to-server means the sensitive, longer-lived access token never appears in browser history, referrer headers, or redirect URLs — only the short-lived, single-use code does, limiting the damage if that code is intercepted. This isn't about raw speed, browsers can technically carry a token in a URL (which is exactly the deprecated implicit grant's flaw), and user authentication still happens regardless of this step.

mcqs.question: Why does PKCE let a public client like a mobile app prove its identity during the code exchange without needing a durable client secret?
options: PKCE eliminates the need for any identity proof during the exchange entirely
The client generates a one-time verifier and sends a hash of it upfront, then proves possession of the original value at exchange time — nothing durable needs to stay secret
PKCE requires the mobile app to store its secret in an encrypted keychain instead
PKCE only works for confidential clients, not public ones
mcqs.explanation: PKCE uses a per-flow, single-use verifier and its hashed challenge instead of a long-lived secret, so there's nothing durable that has to stay hidden inside a public client's code or binary. It doesn't skip identity proof altogether, doesn't rely on secure secret storage on the device, and despite originally targeting public clients, it's now recommended universally including for confidential ones.

mcqs.question: Why was the OAuth implicit grant deprecated in favor of the Authorization Code + PKCE flow?
options: The implicit grant returned the access token directly in the browser redirect URL, exposing it in browser history, referrer headers, and logs
The implicit grant was deprecated purely because it was slower to implement
The implicit grant required users to share their actual password with the Client
The implicit grant has never been supported by any major identity provider
mcqs.explanation: Skipping the code-exchange step meant the access token itself traveled through the browser redirect, landing in history and logs in a way the code-exchange design specifically avoids. Implementation speed wasn't the deprecation driver, sharing the actual password describes the separate Resource Owner Password Credentials grant, and the implicit grant was in fact widely supported before being deprecated.

mcqs.question: A team embeds an OAuth client secret directly in their mobile app's binary, following a tutorial written for server-side web apps. What's wrong with this?
options: Nothing, as long as the binary is code-signed
The secret only matters if the app also stores user passwords locally
Mobile apps are structurally incapable of participating in OAuth flows
The secret can be trivially extracted by decompiling the app, so it was never actually secret — the fix is using PKCE instead of relying on a client secret at all
mcqs.explanation: Anything shipped inside an app binary — including any secret — can be extracted through decompilation, so it provides no real confidentiality regardless of obfuscation; PKCE exists specifically so public clients like mobile apps never need a durable secret at all. Code signing doesn't prevent binary extraction of embedded strings, mobile apps absolutely can and do use OAuth, and this issue is independent of whether the app stores passwords locally.
